prompt: Horta asks 400 of its 9,600 customers about deliveries. Which is the population?

choices.text: The 400 who were asked
choices.why: Those are the sample: the part actually observed.

choices.text: All 9,600 customers
choices.why: Right. The population is the whole group the question is about.

choices.text: Everybody living in Campinas
choices.why: The question is about Horta's customers, not the whole city.

choices.text: The customers who answered
choices.why: Respondents are a subset of the sample, which matters for non-response, but the population is still everyone.

prompt: Match each population parameter to the sample statistic that estimates it.
hint: Greek for the population, Roman for the sample.

prompt: Which statement about a parameter and a statistic is right?
hint: Which of the two is a property of the whole population?

choices.text: Both change from sample to sample
choices.why: The parameter describes the population and stays fixed; only the statistic moves.

choices.text: The parameter is computed from the sample
choices.why: That is the definition of a statistic.

choices.text: A parameter exists only if someone has measured it
choices.why: The true mean of the population exists whether or not anybody knows it.

choices.text: The first stays put; the second moves
choices.why: Right. A different sample gives a different statistic, estimating the same unknown parameter.

prompt: What defines a simple random sample?
hint: Who or what decides who is in it?

choices.text: Every member has the same chance of being chosen
choices.why: Right, and every group of the same size has the same chance too.

choices.text: The analyst picks members who look typical
choices.why: A person choosing introduces their own preferences; random means a chance mechanism decides.

choices.text: Members are taken from the start of the list
choices.why: The start of a list is often sorted by something, such as signup date.

choices.text: It contains at least 30 members
choices.why: Size has nothing to do with whether a sample is random.

prompt: Three random samples of 40 baskets give means of R$ 89.32, R$ 80.03 and R$ 72.47. What does that show?
hint: Would a fourth sample give one of these three means?

choices.text: That one of the samples was drawn wrongly
choices.why: All three were drawn correctly; different random samples give different means.

choices.text: Sample statistics vary from sample to sample
choices.why: Right. That variation is measurable, and lessons 11 and 12 measure it.

choices.text: That random samples are biased
choices.why: Across 1,000 samples the means centred on R$ 82.96, very close to the true R$ 82.78: no lean.

choices.text: That 40 baskets is too few to say anything
choices.why: Forty says something, with a margin of error; it is not nothing.

prompt: Horta draws a perfectly random sample from its customer list, but the list leaves out customers who order by phone. What follows?
hint: Who could have been chosen at all?

choices.text: Nothing, since the draw was random
choices.why: A random draw from an incomplete list cannot reach the people missing from it.

choices.text: The sample is stratified by ordering method
choices.why: Stratifying would include phone customers on purpose; here they are excluded by accident.

choices.text: Its conclusions cover only the customers on the list
choices.why: Right. The sampling frame decides who could be chosen, and phone customers could not.

choices.text: A larger sample would fix it
choices.why: More draws from the same list still never reach phone customers.

prompt: How is a stratified sample drawn?
hint: Every stratum, a random draw in each.

choices.text: By taking every k-th member of a list
choices.why: That is systematic sampling.

choices.text: By choosing a few groups and taking only their members
choices.why: That is cluster sampling.

choices.text: By sampling at random within each group
choices.why: Right. Every stratum contributes, and within each the choice is random.

choices.text: By surveying whoever is easiest to reach in each group
choices.why: That would be a convenience sample in groups, with the same bias.

prompt: Simple random samples of 20 deliveries gave means with a standard deviation of 2.20 minutes, and stratified samples of 20 gave 1.04. By what factor did stratifying reduce it? Give one decimal place.
A survey oversamples business customers, who are 2% of the list, taking 100 of them and 100 households. What must be done before reporting an overall figure?
hint: Half the sample, 2% of the population.

choices.text: Nothing, since both groups were sampled at random
choices.why: Random within groups, but business customers are half the sample and 2% of the population; the plain average overweights them.

choices.text: Weight each group back to its true share
choices.why: Right. Lesson 3's weighted mean: households carry 98% of the weight, business customers 2%.

choices.text: Drop the business customers from the overall figure
choices.why: They are 2% of the population and belong in it, with their proper weight.

choices.text: Draw more households until the groups are equal in the population
choices.why: The population is what it is; sampling cannot change its composition.

prompt: What is the key difference between sampling error and bias?
hint: What happens to each one as the sample grows?

choices.text: Bias is random; sampling error leans one way
choices.why: It is the reverse.

choices.text: Sampling error shrinks with more data; bias does not
choices.why: Right. A biased method gives the same wrong answer more precisely as the sample grows.

choices.text: Bias only happens in small samples
choices.why: The 1936 poll had 2.4 million answers and was badly biased.

choices.text: Sampling error is a mistake by the analyst
choices.why: It is the natural wobble of random samples, not anybody's mistake.

prompt: Match each situation to the kind of bias it shows.
hint: Who chose themselves, who did not answer, who is missing, who was never in reach?

pairs.left: Only customers who chose to tap the rating prompt are counted
Only current customers are asked why they like the shop
Delivery times are measured only on the routes nearest the warehouse

prompt: Near-route deliveries average 31.28 minutes and all deliveries 38.65. By how many minutes does the convenience sample underestimate the mean?
Why did The Literary Digest's 2.4 million ballots in 1936 lose to Gallup's roughly 50,000?
hint: Who owned phones and cars in 1936, and who mailed back a ballot?

choices.text: Gallup's sample was larger in some states
choices.why: It was smaller overall; how the people were chosen was what differed.

choices.text: Mailed ballots are always less accurate than interviews
choices.why: The medium is secondary; the lists and the self-selection were the problem.

choices.text: Too many people changed their minds after the poll
choices.why: Gallup's smaller, better-chosen sample got it right at the same time.

choices.text: Its lists and returns leaned towards better-off voters
choices.why: Right. Selection and voluntary response bias; more answers only made the wrong answer more precise.

prompt: Horta samples its daily records by taking every 7th day. What is the danger?
hint: How many days are in a week?

choices.text: Seven is too large a step
choices.why: The size of the step is not the problem; its match with the weekly cycle is.

choices.text: Every chosen day falls on the same weekday
choices.why: Right. A step that matches the list's rhythm gives an orderly-looking, badly biased sample.

choices.text: Systematic samples cannot have a random start
choices.why: They should have one; it does not fix a matching cycle.

choices.text: Some days will be chosen twice
choices.why: A systematic sample never repeats a member.

prompt: Taking 20 deliveries from one randomly chosen neighbourhood gave sample means with a standard deviation of 9.22 minutes, against 2.20 for a simple random sample of 20. Why?
hint: How many neighbourhoods does each sample see?

choices.text: Cluster samples are biased
choices.why: With the cluster chosen at random they are not biased; they are much more variable.

choices.text: Twenty deliveries is too few in any design
choices.why: The stratified design did very well with 20.

choices.text: Its 20 all come from one area
choices.why: Right. Which neighbourhood came up decides most of the mean, and that is left to a single draw.

choices.text: Neighbourhoods have different numbers of deliveries
choices.why: Here each has 30; the issue is how alike deliveries within one neighbourhood are.

prompt: A random sample of 1,000 is used to describe a city of 1 million and, separately, a country of 200 million. How does the precision compare?
hint: Does the spoonful depend on the size of the pot?

choices.text: The country estimate is 200 times less precise
choices.why: Precision depends on the sample, not on how many were left out.

choices.text: About the same
choices.why: Right. For a sample that is a small fraction of the population, the population's size hardly matters.

choices.text: The city estimate is worse, because 1,000 is a larger share
choices.why: A larger share helps slightly, if anything.

choices.text: Neither is valid below 1% of the population
choices.why: There is no such rule; random samples work at tiny fractions.

prompt: If the wobble of a sample mean shrinks with the square root of the sample size, by what factor must the sample grow to halve it?
hint: Which number has a square root of 2?

prompt: Put the decisions of a survey in the order this lesson recommends.
items: Choose a method that gives everyone a known chance
Draw the sample and collect the answers
trap: Choosing the size first is the commonest mistake: a large sample from a bad method gives a precise wrong answer.
